strengths: The paper addresses a practical NLP question: how much labelled data makes a small specialised model competitive with a larger prompted model. Studying crossing points is more informative than comparing only a few-shot setting with full-data fine-tuning.

Learning curves spanning 10 examples to large training sets, additional measurements near crossing points, and 100 repetitions for most local-model configurations provide a substantial empirical basis. Reporting variation alongside mean macro-F1 is a useful design choice.

The results expose meaningful differences between configurations, including BERT's failure to overtake the prompted models on BoolQ and the strong performance of task-adapted FLAN-T5 with very few additional examples.

The appendix supplies model identifiers, prompts, training settings, and a source-code link. The limitations candidly disclose restricted task coverage, quantisation, smaller evaluation subsets, and fewer ChatGPT repetitions.
weaknesses: Label accounting and evaluation independence are insufficiently established. The limitations describe selecting prompts using 1,000 training and test examples, while early stopping is specified without identifying a validation split. Those selection labels matter to claims about needing only 10 examples. Repartitioning all labelled data also warrants checks for related SST-2 phrases crossing splits and overlap with FLAN-T5's prior instruction-training data. Clarify the partitions, reserve independent evaluation data, and distinguish additional adaptation labels from the full development budget.

The BoolQ prompt in Table 1 asks whether the passage contains an answer to the question. BoolQ instead requires answering the question itself with yes or no; a passage supporting a negative answer still contains an answer. This mismatch can distort the prompted baselines and the conclusions about task complexity. A corrected prompt and targeted reruns are necessary.

The scoring needs a sanity check. Figure 2 places the unexplained 'Random Baseline' near 70 macro-F1 on SST-2 and 60 on MRPC/BoolQ, inconsistent with ordinary label-independent binary guessing, whose population macro-F1 is at most 50. Appendix B also maps unrecognised generations to -1 without specifying whether macro-F1 includes this third label. Define the baseline, document the scorer, and report invalid-output rates before interpreting below-random performance.

The central variance-adjusted thresholds lack a calibrated statistical interpretation. Appendix C uses non-overlap of mean ± one standard deviation to define 'always' better performance; the subsequent caveat does not establish a probability of superiority. Moreover, large models use 1,000 test examples, smaller models use larger test sets, and ChatGPT has six repetitions rather than 100. The resulting dispersions mix evaluation-sampling noise with training or demonstration instability. Comparisons on shared evaluation examples, paired performance differences, and uncertainty estimates for the crossing points would better support the claimed 25–200% increase in required labels.

Training-data size is confounded with optimisation exposure. FLAN-T5 instruction-tuning uses 150 steps with batch size four, so each run processes at most 600 example presentations even when thousands of labels are available. Its flat learning curve therefore does not establish that additional training data offers no benefit. Conversely, fixed-epoch BERT/RoBERTa training receives very few updates in the smallest settings. Validate suitable training schedules and report how many distinct examples each method actually consumes.

The quantitative summary needs correction and tighter qualification. Table 2 reports 1,750 BoolQ examples as 35%, although the stated training pool is approximately 10,000. Appendix C describes an increase from approximately 900 to 1,200 examples as 140%, rather than approximately 33%. The headline 100–1,000 range also understates several important comparisons: SST-2 ICL crossings require 3,000–5,500 examples, and BoolQ requires up to 6,000 for RoBERTa.

The three English binary tasks support a bounded empirical comparison, but do not isolate task complexity as the cause of different thresholds. Likewise, BERT versus RoBERTa confounds parameter count with pretraining differences. This limited generality would not itself prevent Findings acceptance; the decisive obstacles are the evaluation, scoring, and uncertainty concerns above. Addressing them requires reanalysis and targeted reruns, making resubmission next cycle more appropriate than acceptance in the current form.
